solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Axe meant for academic to sell

blocks.note: 'for' and 'to' both mark a purpose or recipient
a Master of Arts, a holder of an academic degree
to hawk goods is to peddle them in the street

explanation.surface: An axe was intended for a lecturer who wanted to sell it on.
explanation.definitionFit: A tomahawk is a light war axe of the Native North Americans.

clue.text: Short tree bird found around lake

indicators.note: a word made short loses its final letter
turning around makes the tree's letters run the other way

blocks.note: a tit is a small songbird
the acacia is a thorny tree

explanation.surface: A bird is found near a stunted tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lake' at the end looks like part of the bird-watching scene, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Titicaca is the large lake on the border of Peru and Bolivia, high in the Andes.

clue.text: Where to trade in a mutant for an alien

indicators.note: a mutant is a changed form, so the words before it change their order

blocks.note: a mart is a market
these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A sci-fi tale where a mutant is swapped at a market for an alien.
explanation.definitionFit: A Martian is a being from Mars, the stock science-fiction alien.

clue.text: What turns a sheep angry

indicators.note: turning the questioning word round makes it read the other way

blocks.note: eh? is said for 'What?'
a tup is a ram

explanation.surface: A puzzled question: what makes a sheep cross?
explanation.walkthrough: 'What turns' looks like the start of a question; in fact What is EH, turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Het up is an informal adjective for agitated or angry, from a dialect past tense of heat.

clue.text: Jockey intends to race, is moving ahead

indicators.note: moving letters around changes their order

blocks.note: will expresses intention
these letters rearranged
on means forward, as in 'go on ahead'

explanation.surface: A jockey plans to race and is already moving to the front.
explanation.walkthrough: Willie Carson is a Scottish former champion flat-racing jockey, later a TV pundit.
explanation.definitionFit: Willie Carson rode five Derby winners and was British champion jockey five times.

clue.text: Short text message about everyone's underwear

indicators.note: about means going round, so the text abbreviation surrounds the next word

blocks.note: SMS is the short message service of mobile phones
everyone is all; the 's is 'is' as a joining word

explanation.surface: Someone texts a quick note about what everybody wears underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short text message' is not a plain description but a pointer to its abbreviation. Smalls is British informal for underclothes.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, smalls are small items of clothing, especially knickers and pants.

clue.text: Ask them if parts may be improvised

indicators.note: the letters part and separate, then come together in a new order

blocks.note: these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Check whether the components might be improvised.
explanation.definitionFit: Makeshift describes something put together as a temporary substitute, improvised from what is to hand.

clue.text: Boy runs alongside a highwayman

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
a means one

explanation.surface: A boy runs next to a highway robber.
explanation.definitionFit: Ladrone is an archaic word, from Spanish, for a robber or bandit, such as a highwayman.

clue.text: Demonstrator in contemptible group

blocks.note: first meaning: one who shows something
second meaning: British slang for a useless bunch

explanation.walkthrough: 'Demonstrator' suggests a protester, but it is simply one who shows; a shower is British slang for a hopeless lot of people.
explanation.definitionFit: A shower is literally one who displays things, and in slang a group held in contempt.

clue.text: Accelerator and choke

blocks.note: first meaning: the valve or pedal controlling an engine's fuel supply
second meaning: to strangle someone

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs two car controls, accelerator and choke; but choke here is the verb to strangle.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is the engine's fuel control; the verb means to squeeze someone's windpipe.

clue.text: Child breaks very old snowmobile

indicators.note: the child breaks into the following word, sitting inside it

blocks.note: so means very, as in 'so good'
a kid is a child
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A child wrecks an antique snow machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaks' suggests damage, but it means the child breaks into the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Skidoo, from the trade name Ski-Doo, is a motorised sledge on tracks, a kind of snowmobile.

clue.text: Spare plastic nuts

blocks.note: plastic means pliable, supple
nuts is slang for crazy, mental

explanation.surface: A list of spare plastic nuts in a hardware drawer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' looks like an anagram signal or hardware, but it means crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Supplemental means additional or extra, as spare can mean surplus to what is needed.

clue.text: X is in when C is out

indicators.note: the named letter is out, so it is dropped from the word it was in

blocks.note: chic means fashionable, which is what 'in' means
the letter itself, to be removed

explanation.surface: A cryptic rule: one letter comes in when another goes out.
explanation.walkthrough: Take CHIC (in) and drop its final C. 'X is in' reads like a rule about letters swapping, but X is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Chi is the Greek letter written as X, so X is the symbol for it.

clue.text: Basic range of camping gear

blocks.note: primus is Latin for first, and in English means chief or basic
a range is a kitchen cooker, a stove

explanation.surface: A shop offers a basic range of equipment for camping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' reads as a selection of products, but it is a cooking range.
explanation.definitionFit: A Primus stove is a portable paraffin burner, standard kit for campers.

clue.text: Rubber housing of one part is set up

indicators.note: a housing encloses something, so one word sits inside another

blocks.note: to contrive is to set up or arrange
an ace is a one in cards
PT is the abbreviation for part

explanation.surface: A rubber casing for a component is installed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubber' sounds like the material, but it is slang for a condom; 'one' as a playing-card ace is a standard crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubber is informal for a condom, the commonest kind of contraceptive.

clue.text: Politely made to pay money into bank

indicators.note: one word goes into another, so it sits inside it

blocks.note: to bank on something is to rely on it
a person fined is made to pay money as a penalty

explanation.surface: Someone is courteously asked to pay money into a bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bank' looks like the place money goes, but it is the verb, as in bank on.
explanation.definitionFit: Refinedly means in a cultured, well-mannered way, much as politely does.

clue.text: Not entirely honest, I'm a terrible judge

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, a run of letters inside it

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning these words

explanation.surface: A confession: to be fair, I'm a dreadful judge of things.
explanation.definitionFit: To estimate is to judge an amount roughly, so the verb judge fits it.

clue.text: Paper of grass, historically?

blocks.note: a grass is slang for a police informer
The Times is a newspaper

explanation.surface: A whimsical question: what newspaper would a grass read?
explanation.walkthrough: Run the answer's first two words together and it reads INFORMER TIMES, the 'paper of a grass'. To grass, in British slang, is to inform on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically means in the past, long ago, which is what in former times says.

clue.text: Strong under pressure, leader's elected

blocks.note: a party elected is in power; leader's puts it first
tense means strained, under pressure

explanation.surface: A strong leader under pressure has been elected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leader's elected' reads as the leader winning; it means the piece for elected comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Intense describes something of great strength or degree, like an intense flavour.

clue.text: Some war paint man mostly used to cover a wound

indicators.note: mostly means not all of the word, so its last letter goes
covering something means going round it, so one part sits inside

blocks.note: taken as written, before trimming
a scar is the mark of a wound
taken as written

explanation.surface: A warrior's face paint is used to hide an injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'War paint' is jokey slang for women's make-up, so the warrior picture is a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Mascara is eye make-up, and war paint is a humorous name for cosmetics.

clue.text: Sign of soccer organisation's intelligence

blocks.note: the FA is the Football Association, with the possessive S
the CIA is the US Central Intelligence Agency

explanation.surface: A sign of how bright football's governing body is.
explanation.walkthrough: The FA runs English football.
explanation.definitionFit: A fascia is the board over a shopfront bearing the shop's name, a kind of sign.

clue.text: Theme park being pulled through changes

indicators.note: the first phrase runs through the middle of the next word, so it sits inside

blocks.note: to alter is to change
a vehicle being pulled is on tow

explanation.surface: A theme park ride drags its riders through twists and turns.
explanation.walkthrough: Alton Towers is a major theme park in Staffordshire, England; 'being pulled' is towing, not a ride's motion.
explanation.definitionFit: Alton Towers is Britain's best-known theme park, with rollercoasters built in an old estate.

clue.text: A beauty's name announced

indicators.note: something announced is spoken, so we go by how the word is said

blocks.note: to cite is to name, quote as an example

explanation.surface: A beauty queen's name is read out on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A beauty' is the definition, a sight worth seeing; 'name' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A sight is a spectacle worth seeing, as in the sights of a city, something beautiful.

clue.text: Short fleece for runner

indicators.note: a word cut short loses its last letter

blocks.note: a fleece is a sheep's skin with the wool on

explanation.surface: A cropped fleece jacket is worn by a jogger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' suggests an athlete, but it is something that runs over snow.
explanation.definitionFit: A ski is a runner, the long narrow strip that slides along snow, like a sledge runner.

clue.text: Country clubs are initially not a thing

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word before it

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
the first letter of are
nada is Spanish-derived slang for nothing

explanation.surface: The country's golf clubs are, at first glance, nothing much.
explanation.definitionFit: Canada is a country in North America, the second largest in the world by area.

clue.text: Test driver felt answer good enough for such marks

definitions.note: the stigmata are the marks; only a holy person is good enough to bear them

blocks.note: The Stig is the anonymous test driver on the TV show Top Gear
to mat is to felt, to tangle fibres into a dense mass
A is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: A test driver sensed his answer was adequate for the scores given.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Felt' reads as the past tense of feel but is the verb to compress fibres. Top Gear is a BBC motoring programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Stigmata are wounds like Christ's that appear on saints, people holy enough to receive them.

clue.text: Yes, I have long fingers

definitions.note: the creature speaks in the first person through the clue's I

blocks.note: aye means yes
the pronoun is spelt as the word that sounds the same

explanation.surface: Someone agrees and mentions their long fingers.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue has the animal speak: 'Yes, I' gives the name, and 'I have long fingers' describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The aye-aye is a Madagascan lemur famous for its very long, thin middle finger used to dig out grubs.

clue.text: Would one share evenly?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone dividing things fairly
setter's reading: flat means even, so this is a person sharing a flat

explanation.walkthrough: 'Evenly' suggests fair division, but flat means level, so the one sharing evenly is sharing a flat.
explanation.definitionFit: A flatmate is someone who shares an apartment, or flat, with another person.
